apa: Lincoln, Y. S., & Guba, E. G. (1985). Naturalistic inquiry. Sage.
annotation: Origin of the trustworthiness framework (credibility, transferability, dependability, confirmability). Cite when justifying rigor criteria as an alternative to validity/reliability.

apa: Miles, M. B., Huberman, A. M., & Saldaña, J. (2020). Qualitative data analysis: A methods sourcebook (4th ed.). Sage.
annotation: The standard sourcebook for displays, matrices, and within-/cross-case analysis. Cite for systematic data management and visualization.

apa: Saldaña, J. (2021). The coding manual for qualitative researchers (4th ed.). Sage.
annotation: The reference catalogue of first- and second-cycle coding methods. Cite to name and justify a specific coding technique.

apa: Glaser, B. G., & Strauss, A. L. (1967). The discovery of grounded theory: Strategies for qualitative research. Aldine. (Routledge reprint, 2017)
annotation: The founding statement of grounded theory and constant comparison. DOI applies to the Routledge reprint. Cite for the origins of inductive theory-building.

apa: Corbin, J., & Strauss, A. (2015). Basics of qualitative research: Techniques and procedures for developing grounded theory (4th ed.). Sage.
annotation: The systematic/procedural strand of grounded theory (open/axial/selective coding). Cite for structured coding paradigms.

apa: Charmaz, K. (2014). Constructing grounded theory (2nd ed.). Sage.
annotation: The constructivist reframing of grounded theory. Cite when foregrounding co-construction and researcher reflexivity.

apa: Patton, M. Q. (2015). Qualitative research & evaluation methods (4th ed.). Sage.
annotation: Comprehensive reference on purposeful sampling and evaluation-oriented design. Cite for sampling logic and applied contexts.

apa: Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101.
annotation: The field-defining six-phase thematic analysis paper. The default citation for any thematic analysis.

apa: Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2019). Reflecting on reflexive thematic analysis. Qualitative Research in Sport, Exercise and Health, 11(4), 589–597.
annotation: Introduces "reflexive TA" and distinguishes it from coding-reliability TA. Cite to specify the reflexive variant.

apa: Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2021). One size fits all? What counts as quality practice in (reflexive) thematic analysis? Qualitative Research in Psychology, 18(3), 328–352.
annotation: Quality criteria for reflexive TA and a critique of misapplications. Cite when defending TA quality.

apa: Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2022). Thematic analysis: A practical guide. Sage.
annotation: The definitive practical manual for reflexive TA. Cite for step-by-step procedure.

apa: Timmermans, S., & Tavory, I. (2012). Theory construction in qualitative research: From grounded theory to abductive analysis. Sociological Theory, 30(3), 167–186.
annotation: The seminal argument that abduction, not pure induction, drives theory construction. Cite to justify an abductive stance.

apa: Tavory, I., & Timmermans, S. (2014). Abductive analysis: Theorizing qualitative research. University of Chicago Press.
annotation: Book-length treatment of abductive analysis. Cite for the full methodology.

apa: Thomas, D. R. (2006). A general inductive approach for analyzing qualitative evaluation data. American Journal of Evaluation, 27(2), 237–246.
annotation: The canonical statement of the "general inductive approach." Cite for a pragmatic inductive coding workflow.

apa: Hsieh, H.-F., & Shannon, S. E. (2005). Three approaches to qualitative content analysis. Qualitative Health Research, 15(9), 1277–1288.
annotation: Distinguishes conventional (inductive), directed (deductive), and summative content analysis. Cite to position your content-analysis approach.

apa: Blumer, H. (1954). What is wrong with social theory? American Sociological Review, 19(1), 3–10.
annotation: Origin of "sensitizing concepts." Cite when using loosely-defined theoretical concepts as analytic starting points.

apa: Stake, R. E. (1995). The art of case study research. Sage.
annotation: Interpretive/intrinsic case study. Cite for holistic, naturalistic case work.

apa: Yin, R. K. (2018). Case study research and applications: Design and methods (6th ed.). Sage.
annotation: The post-positivist case-study design tradition. Cite for propositions, multiple-case logic, and rigor.

apa: Merriam, S. B., & Tisdell, E. J. (2016). Qualitative research: A guide to design and implementation (4th ed.). Jossey-Bass.
annotation: Education-friendly case study and general qualitative design. Cite in education contexts.

apa: Clandinin, D. J., & Connelly, F. M. (2000). Narrative inquiry: Experience and story in qualitative research. Jossey-Bass.
annotation: Founding text of narrative inquiry. Cite for experience-centered, story-based research.

apa: Riessman, C. K. (2008). Narrative methods for the human sciences. Sage.
annotation: Thematic, structural, and dialogic/performance narrative analysis. Cite for narrative analytic techniques.

apa: Smith, J. A., Flowers, P., & Larkin, M. (2022). Interpretative phenomenological analysis: Theory, method and research (2nd ed.). Sage.
annotation: The authoritative IPA manual. Cite for idiographic, experiential phenomenology.

apa: Ritchie, J., & Spencer, L. (1994). Qualitative data analysis for applied policy research. In A. Bryman & R. G. Burgess (Eds.), Analyzing qualitative data (pp. 173–194). Routledge.
annotation: Origin of Framework analysis. DOI applies to the edited volume. Cite for the matrix-based framework approach.

apa: Gale, N. K., Heath, G., Cameron, E., Rashid, S., & Redwood, S. (2013). Using the framework method for the analysis of qualitative data in multi-disciplinary health research. BMC Medical Research Methodology, 13, 117.
annotation: The widely-cited modern operationalization of Framework analysis. Cite for a team-based, stepwise procedure.

apa: Krippendorff, K. (2018). Content analysis: An introduction to its methodology (4th ed.). Sage.
annotation: The standard content-analysis methodology and home of Krippendorff's alpha. Cite for systematic content analysis.

apa: Brown, A. L. (1992). Design experiments: Theoretical and methodological challenges in creating complex interventions in classroom settings. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 2(2), 141–178.
annotation: Founding paper of design experiments. Cite for the origins of design-based research (DBR).

apa: Design-Based Research Collective. (2003). Design-based research: An emerging paradigm for educational inquiry. Educational Researcher, 32(1), 5–8.
annotation: The agenda-setting statement of DBR. Cite to define DBR.

apa: Barab, S., & Squire, K. (2004). Design-based research: Putting a stake in the ground. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 13(1), 1–14.
annotation: Influential framing of DBR's warrants. Cite for DBR's evidentiary claims.

apa: Collins, A., Joseph, D., & Bielaczyc, K. (2004). Design research: Theoretical and methodological issues. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 13(1), 15–42.
annotation: Methodological elaboration of design research. Cite for DBR methodology.

apa: Jordan, B., & Henderson, A. (1995). Interaction analysis: Foundations and practice. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 4(1), 39–103.
annotation: The foundational method for analyzing video records of interaction in the learning sciences. Cite for video/interaction analysis.

apa: American Educational Research Association. (2006). Standards for reporting on empirical social science research in AERA publications. Educational Researcher, 35(6), 33–40.
annotation: The AERA reporting standards. Cite for reporting expectations in education research.

apa: Ladson-Billings, G. (1995). Toward a theory of culturally relevant pedagogy. American Educational Research Journal, 32(3), 465–491.
annotation: Foundational culturally relevant framing. Cite for culturally relevant/responsive methodology in education.

apa: McDonald, N., Schoenebeck, S., & Forte, A. (2019). Reliability and inter-rater reliability in qualitative research: Norms and guidelines for CSCW and HCI practice. Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction, 3(CSCW), Article 72, 1–23.
annotation: The definitive HCI/CSCW treatment of whether and when to use IRR; a meta-analysis finding IRR in ~1/9 of qualitative papers. Cite for reliability norms in HCI.

apa: Dourish, P. (2006). Implications for design. In Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '06) (pp. 541–550). ACM.
annotation: The classic critique of "implications for design" as the metric for ethnography in HCI. Cite on the value of ethnographic/theoretical contributions.

apa: Beyer, H., & Holtzblatt, K. (1998). Contextual design: Defining customer-centered systems. Morgan Kaufmann.
annotation: Source of contextual inquiry and affinity diagramming (the KJ-method lineage). Cite for affinity diagramming/contextual design.

apa: Muller, M. (2014). Curiosity, creativity, and surprise as analytic tools: Grounded theory method. In J. S. Olson & W. A. Kellogg (Eds.), Ways of knowing in HCI (pp. 25–48). Springer.
annotation: Grounded theory adapted for HCI. Cite for GTM in HCI.

apa: Furniss, D., Blandford, A., & Curzon, P. (2011). Confessions from a grounded theory PhD: Experiences and lessons learnt. In Proceedings of CHI 2011 (pp. 113–122). ACM.
annotation: A candid account of doing grounded theory in HCI. Cite for practical GTM guidance.

apa: Zimmerman, J., Forlizzi, J., & Evenson, S. (2007). Research through design as a method for interaction design research in HCI. In Proceedings of CHI '07 (pp. 493–502). ACM.
annotation: Established research through design (RtD) in HCI. Cite to frame design as inquiry.

apa: Gaver, W. (2012). What should we expect from research through design? In Proceedings of CHI '12 (pp. 937–946). ACM.
annotation: Influential argument on RtD's epistemology and rigor. Cite for RtD evaluation.

apa: Blandford, A., Furniss, D., & Makri, S. (2016). Qualitative HCI research: Going behind the scenes. Morgan & Claypool.
annotation: A practical synthesis of qualitative methods for HCI. Cite as an HCI-specific methods primer.

apa: Cohen, J. (1960). A coefficient of agreement for nominal scales. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 20(1), 37–46.
annotation: The original Cohen's kappa. Cite for chance-corrected agreement between two coders on nominal categories.

apa: Cohen, J. (1968). Weighted kappa: Nominal scale agreement with provision for scaled disagreement or partial credit. Psychological Bulletin, 70(4), 213–220.
annotation: Weighted kappa. Cite when disagreements differ in severity (ordered categories).

apa: Fleiss, J. L. (1971). Measuring nominal scale agreement among many raters. Psychological Bulletin, 76(5), 378–382.
annotation: Fleiss' kappa. Cite for 3+ raters where raters are not fixed across items.

apa: Scott, W. A. (1955). Reliability of content analysis: The case of nominal scale coding. Public Opinion Quarterly, 19(3), 321–325.
annotation: Scott's pi. Cite as the predecessor to kappa using a joint (rather than individual) chance distribution.

apa: Hayes, A. F., & Krippendorff, K. (2007). Answering the call for a standard reliability measure for coding data. Communication Methods and Measures, 1(1), 77–89.
annotation: The accessible standard reference for Krippendorff's alpha (any measurement level, ≥2 coders, missing data). Cite when you need one flexible coefficient.

apa: Feinstein, A. R., & Cicchetti, D. V. (1990). High agreement but low kappa: I. The problems of two paradoxes. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 43(6), 543–549.
annotation: Defines the kappa paradox. Cite to explain why kappa can be low despite high observed agreement.

apa: Cicchetti, D. V., & Feinstein, A. R. (1990). High agreement but low kappa: II. Resolving the paradoxes. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 43(6), 551–558.
annotation: The companion "resolution" paper. Cite for the recommended positive/negative agreement diagnostics.

apa: Gwet, K. L. (2008). Computing inter-rater reliability and its variance in the presence of high agreement. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 61(1), 29–48.
annotation: Introduces the AC1/AC2 statistics that resist the prevalence/paradox problem. Cite when prevalence is skewed.

apa: Shrout, P. E., & Fleiss, J. L. (1979). Intraclass correlations: Uses in assessing rater reliability. Psychological Bulletin, 86(2), 420–428.
annotation: The foundational ICC typology (six forms). Cite to choose an ICC model.

apa: McGraw, K. O., & Wong, S. P. (1996). Forming inferences about some intraclass correlation coefficients. Psychological Methods, 1(1), 30–46.
annotation: Extends and clarifies ICC inference. Cite alongside Shrout & Fleiss for ICC selection. (Correction in Psychological Methods, 1(4), 390.)

apa: Koo, T. K., & Li, M. Y. (2016). A guideline of selecting and reporting intraclass correlation coefficients for reliability research. Journal of Chiropractic Medicine, 15(2), 155–163.
annotation: The practical decision guide for the 10 ICC forms and interpretation bands. Cite for ICC selection and reporting.

apa: Landis, J. R., & Koch, G. G. (1977). The measurement of observer agreement for categorical data. Biometrics, 33(1), 159–174.
annotation: Source of the widely-used magnitude bands (Slight/Fair/Moderate/Substantial/Almost Perfect). Cite when interpreting kappa/alpha — but note the thresholds are explicitly arbitrary heuristics.

apa: Hallgren, K. A. (2012). Computing inter-rater reliability for observational data: An overview and tutorial. Tutorials in Quantitative Methods for Psychology, 8(1), 23–34.
annotation: A hands-on tutorial (with SPSS/R) for choosing and computing kappa and ICC. Cite for practical computation.

apa: O'Connor, C., & Joffe, H. (2020). Intercoder reliability in qualitative research: Debates and practical guidelines. International Journal of Qualitative Methods, 19, 1–13.
annotation: Reviews the arguments for/against intercoder reliability and gives practical guidelines. Cite to decide whether ICR fits your study.

apa: Birt, L., Scott, S., Cavers, D., Campbell, C., & Walter, F. (2016). Member checking: A tool to enhance trustworthiness or merely a nod to validation? Qualitative Health Research, 26(13), 1802–1811.
annotation: Critical, practical treatment of member checking. Cite when designing respondent validation.

apa: Denzin, N. K. (2012). Triangulation 2.0. Journal of Mixed Methods Research, 6(2), 80–88.
annotation: Denzin's updated statement on triangulation. Cite for the concept's contemporary meaning.

apa: Guest, G., Bunce, A., & Johnson, L. (2006). How many interviews are enough? An experiment with data saturation and variability. Field Methods, 18(1), 59–82.
annotation: The most-cited empirical study of saturation; found saturation within the first twelve interviews. Cite for sample-size justification.

apa: Saunders, B., Sim, J., Kingstone, T., Baker, S., Waterfield, J., Bartlam, B., Burroughs, H., & Jinks, C. (2018). Saturation in qualitative research: Exploring its conceptualization and operationalization. Quality & Quantity, 52(4), 1893–1907.
annotation: Clarifies competing meanings of saturation. Cite to specify which saturation you mean.

apa: Malterud, K., Siersma, V. D., & Guassora, A. D. (2016). Sample size in qualitative interview studies: Guided by information power. Qualitative Health Research, 26(13), 1753–1760.
annotation: Proposes "information power" as an alternative to saturation. Cite for a more defensible sample-size rationale.

apa: Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2021). To saturate or not to saturate? Questioning data saturation as a useful concept for thematic analysis and sample-size rationales. Qualitative Research in Sport, Exercise and Health, 13(2), 201–216.
annotation: The reflexive-TA critique of saturation. Cite when rejecting saturation logic in interpretivist work.

apa: National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research. (1979). The Belmont Report: Ethical principles and guidelines for the protection of human subjects of research. U.S. Department of Health & Human Services.
annotation: The foundational U.S. statement of research ethics — respect for persons, beneficence, justice. Cite for the principles underlying IRB review.

apa: Brandt, A. M. (1978). Racism and research: The case of the Tuskegee syphilis study. The Hastings Center Report, 8(6), 21–29.
annotation: The definitive scholarly account of the Tuskegee study and its ethical failures. Cite when invoking Tuskegee as motivation for human-subjects protections.

apa: Chambers, C. D., & Tzavella, L. (2022). The past, present and future of Registered Reports. Nature Human Behaviour, 6(1), 29–42.
annotation: The definitive overview of Registered Reports, where a study is peer-reviewed and accepted on its question and design before any data are collected. Cite for the principle that a study should be worth doing regardless of how the results turn out.

apa: Nosek, B. A., Ebersole, C. R., DeHaven, A. C., & Mellor, D. T. (2018). The preregistration revolution. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 115(11), 2600–2606.
annotation: Argues for committing hypotheses and an analysis plan in advance to keep confirmatory and exploratory work distinct. Cite when teaching students to write the analysis plan before collecting data.

apa: Fetters, M. D., Curry, L. A., & Creswell, J. W. (2013). Achieving integration in mixed methods designs—Principles and practices. Health Services Research, 48(6pt2), 2134–2156.
annotation: How to actually integrate qualitative and quantitative strands—connecting, building, merging, and joint displays—rather than reporting them side by side. Cite for why a joint display yields a takeaway (confirmation, expansion, or discordance) regardless of the statistical result.

apa: McCauley, R., Fitzgerald, S., Lewandowski, G., Murphy, L., Simon, B., Thomas, L., & Zander, C. (2008). Debugging: A review of the literature from an educational perspective. Computer Science Education, 18(2), 67–92.
annotation: A review synthesizing decades of debugging-education research — a good 'anchor tome' to read deeply and snowball from. Cite as the map of the debugging-education area.

apa: Fitzgerald, S., Lewandowski, G., McCauley, R., Murphy, L., Simon, B., Thomas, L., & Zander, C. (2008). Debugging: Finding, fixing and flailing, a multi-institutional study of novice debuggers. Computer Science Education, 18(2), 93–116.
annotation: Multi-institution study of how novices actually debug (often 'flailing' without a plan). Cite for evidence on novice debugging behavior; a natural snowball from McCauley et al.

apa: Loksa, D., Ko, A. J., Jernigan, W., Oleson, A., Mendez, C. J., & Burnett, M. M. (2016). Programming, problem solving, and self-awareness: Effects of explicit guidance. In Proceedings of the 2016 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (pp. 1449–1461). Association for Computing Machinery.
annotation: Explicit metacognitive guidance improves novices' programming problem-solving. Cite as the basis for a metacognitive-prompt intervention.

apa: Aleven, V., Stahl, E., Schworm, S., Fischer, F., & Wallace, R. (2003). Help seeking and help design in interactive learning environments. Review of Educational Research, 73(3), 277–320.
annotation: Foundational review of help-seeking in tutoring systems — help offered is not the same as help used. Cite as an adjacent-domain analogy for CS help-seeking.

apa: Karabenick, S. A., & Newman, R. S. (Eds.). (2006). Help seeking in academic settings: Goals, groups, and contexts. Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.
annotation: Anchor volume on academic help-seeking as a self-regulated learning strategy (help avoidance as a threat response). Cite for the motivation-psychology framing of help-seeking.
